solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Very small duck, nothing to write home about

blocks.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a tiny duckling as unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' for O comes from cricket, where a batter out without scoring makes a duck, written as a zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe something merely mediocre, neither good nor bad, an idiom for unimpressive quality.

clue.text: One often depressed astronaut hitting the bottle here?

definitions.text: One often depressed astronaut hitting the bottle here?

blocks.note: surface reading: a gloomy person; setter's reading: a keyboard key that gets pushed down constantly
setter's reading: a drinking place for someone in orbit, a pub beyond the atmosphere

explanation.surface: A miserable astronaut drowns their sorrows at some drinking spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed' means pressed down, not sad: the long key at the bottom of a keyboard is pressed more than any other, and read literally its name is a pub in orbit.
explanation.definitionFit: The long keyboard key typing gaps between words is pressed constantly, and jokingly it names a drinking venue for cosmonauts.

clue.text: Walk proudly in support

blocks.note: first meaning: to swagger along
second meaning: a brace or bar holding up a structure

explanation.surface: Someone parades with pride while backing a cause.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb and the noun share a spelling but are unrelated senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means swaggering with chest out; the noun is a rigid rod bracing a framework, like those in aircraft wings.

clue.text: Queen Victoria was said to be so disapproving

definitions.text: Queen Victoria was said to be so

blocks.clueFragment: Queen Victoria was said to be so
blocks.note: first meaning: a reference to the famous remark attributed to her, 'We are not amused'
second meaning: showing displeasure

explanation.surface: A historical note on the old queen's stern temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Victoria, Britain's monarch 1837-1901, is reputed to have said 'We are not amused'; the clue leans on that quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not entertained by a joke or behaviour shows displeasure, a near synonym for frowning disapproval.

clue.text: Poor to benefit more? At last!

indicators.note: poor means badly made or in bad shape, so the following letters are in a defective order

blocks.note: the thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A social-justice cry that the poor should finally gain more, greeted with relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is the anagram signal working on the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Both exclamations greet something arriving after a long wait, an idiom meaning it should have come sooner.

clue.text: Power of small child proclaimed

indicators.note: proclaiming is announcing out loud, so we want the sound of the word rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a mite is a tiny child, and spoken it matches a word for strength

explanation.surface: A toddler's strength is loudly announced.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'mite' is an affectionate word for a very small child.
explanation.definitionFit: Strength or force is a straightforward synonym, as in 'with all his strength'.

clue.text: Famous actor set up new company

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom, which turns the letters around

blocks.note: a celebrated performer is a star
to set something somewhere is to put it there

explanation.surface: A celebrity launches their own business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' reads as one phrase meaning founded, but 'set' supplies letters and 'up' reverses them in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A young business just launched, often a tech venture, is the standard term for a fledgling enterprise.

clue.text: Profound part of nationwide epidemic

indicators.note: a part of something is a portion inside it, so the letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A serious aspect of a national outbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the end of 'nationwide' and the start of 'epidemic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep thoughts are profound ones; both adjectives describe great intellectual or emotional depth.

clue.text: Beetle son caught — one from Egypt?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
an Egyptian is one example of an Arab, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A boy captures an insect, perhaps an Egyptian one.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Arab is only an example of a person from Egypt; the beetle itself was sacred in ancient Egypt, adding to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The sacred dung beetle of ancient Egypt is a specific kind of insect in this order, so this is an example relation.

clue.text: Cut up nearly all tropical fruit

indicators.note: nearly all means everything short of the whole, so the final letter goes
cutting something up breaks it into bits that can be rearranged

blocks.note: the word with its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: Someone chops up most of a tropical fruit for a salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tropical fruit' looks like the definition, but 'tropical' is the fodder, and the answer is not even tropical.
explanation.definitionFit: This orange stone fruit related to the peach is a specific example of something edible grown on trees.

clue.text: Look around lake for cover

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to gaze is to look steadily
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Someone scans the lakeside looking for shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests shelter, but here it is a verb for coating something with a shiny layer.
explanation.definitionFit: To glaze pottery or a pastry is to coat its surface with a glossy layer, a sense of the verb to coat.

clue.text: Go into hospital department? I’m not sure

blocks.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department
er is the hesitant sound someone makes when unsure

explanation.surface: A nervous patient hesitates about being admitted to a ward.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the clue: the hesitation itself becomes the letters of the hesitant noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Going into a room or building is a plain synonym for coming inside it.

clue.text: What one might inherit from European country

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a nation is a state

explanation.surface: A legacy left behind from some country on the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a single synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead person's property and assets pass to heirs, and a landed property is likewise passed down through families.

clue.text: Prey seen all over the place in these mountains

indicators.note: scattered all over the place means in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wild animals to hunt are spotted everywhere in some mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'These mountains' points to a range whose name is made from the scattered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The range forming the border between France and Spain is a particular example of a mountain chain.

clue.text: A DIY book?

blocks.note: surface reading: a manual on home repairs and carpentry
setter's reading: do it yourself, a life story written by its own subject

explanation.walkthrough: DIY means do-it-yourself, usually home improvement; here it is the life story that the subject wrote personally.
explanation.definitionFit: A memoir written by the person it describes is literally a self-made biography, hence the do-it-yourself label.

clue.text: Article right about pub becoming solvent

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so these letters go around another piece

blocks.note: the definite article
R is the abbreviation for right
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about a pub that turns out to be financially sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solvent' suggests able to pay debts, but here it is the liquid that dissolves or dilutes paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Paint thinner, such as turpentine or white spirit, is a liquid that dissolves substances, the chemical sense of solvent.

clue.text: Cause of betrayal initially disregarded

indicators.note: the opening letter is ignored, so it drops off the front

blocks.note: treason is betrayal of one's country

explanation.surface: The motive behind a betrayal was overlooked at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' here selects the first letter for removal, not the first letter to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: A cause of something is the grounds or motive for it, a direct synonym of the noun.

clue.text: Time to give out paper hanky

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to issue is to distribute or hand out

explanation.surface: It is time to hand out handkerchiefs to someone in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: A hanky is a handkerchief; the paper sort has its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: A disposable sheet of soft absorbent stuff used for blowing your nose replaces the cloth handkerchief.

clue.text: Town’s WI nearly smothering scoundrel

indicators.note: to smother is to cover completely, so the earlier words wrap around and conceal the letters

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the third

explanation.surface: The local Women's Institute almost suffocates a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI is the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women; the hidden letters start with the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a pig is an insult for a contemptible, unpleasant person, an informal synonym for rogue.

clue.text: Conscious of conflict in A&E

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the two letters either side of the ampersand
a war is an armed conflict

explanation.surface: A doctor notices a fight breaking out in the emergency ward.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E, accident and emergency, is the British name for a hospital emergency room; here its two letters frame the middle piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing about something or having knowledge of it is the same as being mindful of it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Gather a large number

blocks.note: taken as written
a great heap or quantity

explanation.surface: Collect lots of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one instruction, but it is definition first and then a two-part build.
explanation.definitionFit: To accumulate or collect over time is to pile up, a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Takes drugs, American drugs

blocks.note: US is short for the United States
the second occurrence: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so several are Es

explanation.surface: Someone on drugs, specifically American ones.
explanation.walkthrough: E for ecstasy is a common crossword convention; the definition takes in the first 'drugs' as part of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who regularly consumes illegal substances is said to be a user, so the verb carries this slang sense.

clue.text: Muslim of a cheerful disposition, some might say

indicators.note: what people say is spoken, so it is the sound of the phrase that counts

blocks.note: a cheerful temperament is a bright one

explanation.surface: A description of a good-humoured believer.
explanation.walkthrough: The cheerful adjective and the branch of Islam are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the larger of the two main branches of Islam is a particular kind of follower of that faith.

clue.text: Press agency reduced by 50 per cent? It was a long time ago

definitions.text: It was a long time ago

indicators.note: cutting by half leaves only half the letters, so the back half goes

blocks.note: to press clothes is to iron them
the first half of the word, three of its six letters, once the back half is cut

explanation.surface: A news or press agency being slashed in size, recalled as something long past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press agency' reads as one news organisation, but 'press' is the clothes-smoothing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The prehistoric period after the Bronze Age, when people first smelted the metal, lies far in the past.

clue.text: Unruly kids here screamed

indicators.note: unruly means out of control, so the letters break out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Rowdy children yelled at the top of their voices.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a complete sentence, so 'Unruly' passes as a plain description of the children.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe crying out in a high piercing voice, direct synonyms in the past tense.

clue.text: Rock band cancelling opening in current circumstances

indicators.note: cancelling the opening removes the beginning, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: Oasis was a famous Manchester rock group of the 1990s

explanation.surface: A rock group calls off its first gig in the present situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' sounds like a gig or a premiere, but it is the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Selling something as is means in its present state without changes, matching the phrase about existing conditions.
